title: Job loses everything
hookLine: a good man loses his children, wealth and health (Job 1–2)

lines: A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.
cards: "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." The book opens like a folk tale.
Before anything happens to him, it tells us what kind of man he is: "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Hold on to that line; the whole book leans on it.
The story is about to take everything this man has, and it wants the reader to know, before a single loss, that he did nothing to earn it.

teach.h: A FULL HOUSE, A CAREFUL FATHER.
teach.b: First, a full house. Job has sons and daughters, flocks and herds, and a large household.
His children hold feasts in each other's homes, and afterward Job rises early to make offerings for them, in case one of them sinned in their heart.

Second, a scene Job never sees. The story moves to heaven, and a figure the King James calls Satan puts a question to God: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Take away what he has, the figure says, and see what he does.
God allows it. Nowhere in the book is Job told about this conversation.
Third, the messengers. On one day messengers come running, each still speaking when the next arrives. Raiders took the oxen and the donkeys.
Fire fell and burned the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And a great wind struck the house where his sons and daughters were eating, and they died.
Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and says: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

Then chapter two takes his body too: sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head. He sits down among the ashes and scrapes himself with a piece of broken pottery. Fourth, it wasn't deserved.
The book tells the reader, and not Job, that none of this is punishment.

God himself calls Job his servant, a perfect and an upright man. Jews and Christians both read Job as scripture, and they read it in many ways. But the book itself starts here: a good man, and losses he did not earn.

how: Jews and Christians read the book of Job as scripture, and it is often read or studied in times of grief and loss; readers in both traditions interpret its opening in different ways.

o: a man punished for a hidden sin he finally confesses
a blameless man who loses everything, not as punishment
a prophet who warned a city of a coming disaster

games.q: inside Job's first chapters — tap the pairs.
p: doth Job fear God for nought?
each speaking as the next arrives
what Job scrapes his sores with

s: the opening of Job presents his losses as punishment
it calls him perfect and upright, and God calls him his servant.
Job is told about the conversation in heaven
the reader hears it; Job never does.
after the first losses, Job blesses the name of the LORD

games.q: you're Job. messenger after messenger: the oxen, the sheep, the camels, and then your children. what do you do?
o: demand that the messengers explain why
tear your robe, fall to the ground, and bless the name of the LORD
games.why: he mourns, falls to the ground, and says the LORD gave and the LORD hath taken away. his arguments come later.

practice: Bring to mind someone carrying a pain they didn't earn, an illness, an accident, a loss out of nowhere; it might be you.

Picture them as the book pictures Job, sitting down in the ashes with what's left, and be the reader who knows what Job is not told: say inwardly, once, slowly, it wasn't deserved. Then just stay beside them.

wordCard.voice: Job, the blameless man from the land of Uz who loses his children, his wealth and his health, though the reader is told it isn't punishment. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Job, the man from the land of Uz, as his name is written in the Hebrew Bible.
